title: Peer review is overwhelmed—can it survive in the AI era?
gist: Academic peer review is buckling as indexed papers grow 5.6% annually while reviewer supply collapses — one immunology editor now emails ~30 researchers to land a single reviewer versus 5-10 emails for three reviewers five years ago — and over half of reviewers already use AI, sometimes producing hallucinated citations. AI researchers are exiting first to blogs and the AI Alignment Forum's upvote-based system, with under 50% of citation-worthy ML work now formally peer reviewed; the base case is not collapse but dilution, with panels shrinking from three reviewers to two, paid review at $100-300 spreading, and journal proliferation forced to curb.

insights.claim: Papers indexed in Scopus and Web of Science are growing exponentially at roughly 5.6 percent per year, outrunning the volunteer reviewer pool that validates them.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Compounding submission volume is the demand driver for any paid-review, AI-review or publishing-infrastructure business; watch submission counts as the top-line KPI for the sector.
insights.quote: The number of papers indexed in the databases Scopus and Web of Science, for example, has recently been increasing exponentially, at a rate of 5.6 percent per year.
insights.locator: Ars Video The number of papers indexed

insights.claim: Global peer review consumes an estimated 15,000 person-years of researcher labor annually, worth about $1.5 billion for the US share alone if it were paid.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Quantifies the unpriced subsidy publishers extract from academia — the size of the value pool that reviewer-payment or AI-assisted review would monetize or displace.
insights.quote: researchers around the globe are devoting a collective 15,000 years of work to peer review every year—work that, if paid, would cost $1.5 billion for the share done in the US alone
insights.locator: By one estimate, researchers around the globe

insights.claim: Finding reviewers has degraded roughly six-fold in five years: a Human Immunology editor now emails about thirty researchers to land one reviewer, versus five to 10 emails to land three reviewers five years ago.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: A concrete, dated measure of system decay — the clearest leading indicator that journal throughput and quality control are breaking.
insights.quote: has recently had to email around thirty researchers to find just one who would review a paper. Five years ago, he estimates it would have taken only five to 10 emails to find three willing reviewers.
insights.locator: Steven Mack, an editor for Human Immunology

insights.claim: Active researchers report receiving roughly 10 review requests a month against capacity for one or two, and journal editors respond by assigning reviews to people who are unqualified or too busy to do them properly.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Quality erosion is structural, not anecdotal — expect rising retraction and error rates in the published literature, a tailwind for research-integrity tooling.
insights.quote: it’s not surprising that editors are assigning reviews to people who aren’t qualified or don’t have the time to concentrate on them
insights.locator: In this landscape, it’s not surprising

insights.claim: Single-reviewer decisions are becoming failure points: an HPV-vaccine-mandate policy study was rejected outright after its lone reviewer confused a study of policy effectiveness with a challenge to vaccine efficacy, with no second reviewer to correct the error.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Illustrates variance risk in gatekeeping — thinner review panels mean publication outcomes increasingly reflect noise, weakening peer review as a quality signal buyers rely on.
insights.quote: Often, papers are reviewed by two or three experts, so if one misunderstands, the others can add clarity. But in this case, there was only one reviewer, so the paper was rejected.
insights.locator: Often, papers are reviewed by two or three experts

insights.claim: Journal proliferation between 1960 and 2020, the shift to online-only publishing that removed page-count limits, and recurring 'special issues' have structurally expanded publishing capacity independent of research quality.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Supply of publication slots, not demand for knowledge, drives volume — so any correction must come through journal consolidation, which is the author's stated endgame.
insights.quote: Many journals are also publishing more manuscripts because they’re now online-only, which frees editors from having to fit an issue onto a limited amount of paper.
insights.locator: That cadence comes in part because more people

insights.claim: AI is a double-sided load on peer review: it lowers the cost of writing up work and lets non-English-native researchers submit to English-language journals, raising submission volume while adding no reviewer capacity.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Generative AI asymmetrically inflates content supply versus verification capacity — the same imbalance that will hit every gatekept content market, not just science.
insights.quote: AI contributes to the overload by making it easier for researchers to write up their work and easier for people from around the globe to submit to English-language journals.
insights.locator: Research is also increasingly interdisciplinary

insights.claim: Paper mills — services that sell authorship on fabricated but legitimate-looking publications — now form a paid adversarial layer feeding submissions into an already saturated review system.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: A funded fraud supply chain against an unfunded volunteer defense is a losing arms race; screening/detection tooling becomes a required cost line for publishers.
insights.quote: Then there are paper mills, or services that charge desperate researchers a fee to put their names on fabricated (but often legitimate-looking) publications.
insights.locator: Then there are paper mills

insights.claim: An editorial-board member of Wiley's Learned Publishing argues the sector needs explicit 'de-growth' of publishing rather than more capacity, calling the growth 'extremely unhealthy'.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: A degrowth norm inside the publishing establishment would compress the article-volume economics that underpin open-access APC revenue models.
insights.quote: Sometimes I think we need to start talking about the de-growth of publishing
insights.locator: All of this has made it difficult

themes.theme: Peer review as a legitimacy product, not a scientific method

insights.claim: Universal peer review is only about 50 years old, despite being treated as the defining feature of legitimate science, meaning the current system is a recent institutional artifact rather than a permanent fixture.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Frames peer review as a replaceable institution — reduces the perceived risk of alternative validation models and the moat of incumbent journals.
insights.quote: peer review has been a universal feature of academic publishing for only about 50 years
insights.locator: Despite its central position in today’s research culture

insights.claim: Peer review became universal as a political-legitimacy defense: with the 1970s US economy tanking and the National Science Foundation under pressure to justify spending, independent review panels gave funding decisions an air of legitimacy that kept lawmakers from taking direct political control.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Explains why the system survives despite dysfunction — its real function is insulating budgets from politics, so reform will be resisted wherever public funding is politically exposed.
insights.quote: It was really, in a lot of ways, a sales pitch from scientists to other stakeholders that made peer review into this cornerstone of science
insights.locator: Peer review became universal almost accidentally

insights.claim: The UK adopted the same legitimacy framing in the late 1980s and early 1990s, when controversies over HIV, autism causation and cold fusion pushed scientific organizations to define proper science as peer-reviewed science.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Peer review's status is demand-driven by public trust crises — expect the label to be defended hardest precisely when misinformation pressure is highest.
insights.quote: We can tell what proper science looks like because proper science is peer reviewed
insights.locator: The United Kingdom went through a similar moment

insights.claim: The volunteer model was built for an era when researchers were independent gentlemen whose publishing was not tied to career progression, so free reviewing worked; tying publication to jobs and grants broke the incentive that sustained it.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: The labor model is mismatched to modern incentives — payment or AI substitution is the only way the accounting closes.
insights.quote: Researchers were independent gentlemen rather than university professors, so publishing wasn’t tied to career progression.
insights.locator: Researchers were independent gentlemen

themes.theme: AI research is defecting to blogs and forums

insights.claim: Submissions to top AI conferences have risen between two- and ten-fold since 2019, producing reviews from people who do not understand the field well enough to evaluate the work.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Conference peer review is already the least reliable filter in the fastest-moving technical field — investors reading AI claims cannot lean on the peer-reviewed label.
insights.quote: the number of papers submitted to top AI conferences has increased between two- and 10-fold since 2019
insights.locator: AI researchers are feeling the content explosion

insights.claim: Because much AI work happens outside academia, researchers there don't need formal publications for career progression, which is why blogs have become a credible primary publication venue in that field specifically.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Corporate employment breaks the journal lock-in — the exit from peer review will spread to whichever fields industrialize next, eroding journal pricing power there.
insights.quote: Their field is new, it’s moving lightning-fast, and much of the work is taking place outside academia, so many researchers don’t need formal publications for their career progression.
insights.locator: AI researchers are well-positioned to experiment

insights.claim: Reputation in AI now accrues through distribution rather than through gatekeepers, with a well-maintained blog described as functionally equivalent to a good podcast channel for amplifying a researcher's voice.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Attention, not accreditation, is the scarce asset in AI — sourcing edge means monitoring individual blogs and forums, not journal tables of contents.
insights.quote: maintaining a good blog is almost like having a good podcast channel
insights.locator: Against this backdrop, blogs have taken off

insights.claim: By one practitioner's estimate, less than 50 percent of the work worth citing in a machine learning paper is properly peer reviewed, and reviewers in most disciplines have come to accept non-peer-reviewed citations within about five years.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: The peer-reviewed corpus is no longer the state of the art in ML — due diligence on AI claims must go to preprints, forums and blogs or it misses most of the field.
insights.quote: I think less than 50 percent of things you really want to cite in [a machine learning] paper end up actually being properly peer reviewed
insights.locator: Five years ago, this was a bigger problem

insights.claim: The AI Alignment Forum replaces peer review with upvotes, downvotes and comments plus an annual retrospective in which members write commentaries on whether the year's top claims have held up over time.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: A working template for post-publication, revisable peer review — the mechanism to copy if you're building or backing an alternative validation layer.
insights.quote: Another way the AI Alignment Forum tries to highlight quality work is by revisiting the year’s top content and asking members to write commentaries on how it’s aged and whether the claims have held up.
insights.locator: On the other hand, posts tend to get many more reactions

insights.claim: The stated case for community voting over social media is control of a field's attention: without it, research salience becomes downstream of proprietary, opaque and potentially biased platform recommendation algorithms.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Whoever owns the ranking layer for scientific attention captures the function journals used to hold — a structurally valuable position currently sitting with social platforms by default.
insights.quote: I really don’t want the attention of my field to be downstream of the Twitter algorithm
insights.locator: But that puts a field’s focus at the whim of companies

insights.claim: Abandoning peer review carries a citation-isolation cost: researchers who publish only in peer-reviewed venues cannot cite forum-published work without raising red flags, cutting them off from a large segment of their own field.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: The literature is bifurcating into two non-interoperable pools, which slows knowledge diffusion and makes field-level surveys systematically incomplete.
insights.quote: That means he can’t cite a large segment of the work in his field. “It’s incredibly limiting,”
insights.locator: That poses a problem for Thorstad

insights.claim: Colloquial blog-style publishing risks trading rigor for accessibility and letting charismatic voices rise regardless of work quality, an explicit counterweight to the pro-blog case.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Charisma-weighted selection is a new source of systematic error in AI discourse — discount claims that travel on personality rather than replication.
insights.quote: accessibility could come at the expense of rigor and that colloquial writing could let charismatic voices rise to the top regardless of the quality of their work
insights.locator: But philosopher David Thorstad from Vanderbilt University cautions

insights.claim: A survey by staff at the Frontiers journals found that over half of peer reviewers already incorporate AI into the review process in some way.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: AI is already the de facto reviewer at the majority of the workflow — the market question is who supplies the sanctioned tool, not whether AI is used.
insights.quote: A survey conducted by staff at the Frontiers journals found that over half of peer reviewers already incorporate AI into the process in some way
insights.locator: With peer review still taking up a lot of time

insights.claim: AI-generated reviews are already imposing real costs on authors: a Leiden linguist spent two days hunting a hallucinated medieval Arabic citation before AI-detection tools and tells such as gratuitous em dashes confirmed the review was machine-written.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Hallucinated citations transfer verification cost onto authors, which is exactly the failure mode that will force journals to buy provenance and detection tooling.
insights.quote: It was very frustrating and a colossal waste of my time
insights.locator: But he couldn’t track down the reference anywhere

insights.claim: Uploading an unpublished manuscript to a chatbot that retains data may constitute a breach of confidentiality, and the proposed fixes — local LLMs or no-retention services — require care from exactly the people already taking shortcuts.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Creates demand for on-prem/no-retention inference in academic publishing, and a compliance risk that could trigger journal-level AI policies and enterprise contracts.
insights.quote: uploading an unpublished manuscript to a chatbot that may retain the data could constitute a breach of confidentiality
insights.locator: In addition to the risk of hallucinations

insights.claim: NeurIPS is running a trial this year of a custom AI tool designed to help reviewers understand submissions and do background research without writing the review itself, an explicit assistive-not-substitutive design boundary.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: A high-profile venue defining the sanctioned scope of AI in review sets the template others will copy — watch the trial's outcome as the reference point for compliant AI-review products.
insights.quote: the tool could help researchers understand the submission and do the background research necessary to write the review, but it would not write the review itself
insights.locator: This year, the AI conference NeurIPS will run a trial

themes.theme: Reform levers with evidence behind them

insights.claim: There is evidence that paying reviewers $100–$300 per review speeds up the process without compromising quality, plausibly because money converts a soft deadline into a hard one.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: A concrete price point for reviewer labor — the number to model against publication fees when assessing whether paid review is economically viable at scale.
insights.quote: There is evidence that compensation in the $100–$300 range per review speeds up the process without compromising quality.
insights.locator: Some researchers also advocate for paying peer reviewers

insights.claim: Portable peer review — a community reviews papers before journal submission, and multiple committed journals accept that review — lets rejected authors move to a second journal without a fresh review round, and is already in limited use.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Decoupling review from the journal breaks the bundle that gives publishers pricing power; it is the structural change with the largest potential effect on publisher economics.
insights.quote: If the first journal decides not to publish an article, the authors can approach a second journal without having to undergo a new round of peer review.
insights.locator: One option, which is already in use on a limited basis

insights.claim: Preprints on sites such as arxiv.org are now accepted as a legitimate basis for grant and job applications in some fields, on the reasoning that careers shouldn't pause while formal publication grinds through.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Career credit has already partially migrated off the journal — the underlying demand for formal publication is weaker than headline submission counts suggest.
insights.quote: Preprints are now seen as a legitimate basis for grant and job applications in some fields
insights.locator: One long-standing tactic to address the slow review process

insights.claim: Review workload is distributed inequitably rather than in proportion to submissions, with editors disproportionately assigning reviews to male researchers in the United States and a handful of other countries.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: There is latent reviewer capacity outside the over-tapped cohort — a cheap operational fix journals can pull before resorting to payment or AI.
insights.quote: Editors tend to disproportionately assign reviews to male researchers from the United States and a handful of other countries rather than distributing the workload equitably.
insights.locator: One obvious step is to redistribute the review workload

insights.claim: A scholarly communication advocate argues that most journal articles don't need peer review at all, and that papers should have to clear a threshold of interest before consuming reviewer time, given how few papers end up having an impact.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Triage-before-review would slash review demand overnight and reprice the peer-reviewed label as a scarce premium tier rather than a default stamp.
insights.quote: Maybe, he suggests, studies should have to meet a threshold of interest before they’re sent out for peer review.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, scholarly communication advocate Cameron Neylon

insights.claim: The stated forecast is not the abolition of peer review but its dilution: with reviewer pools tapped out, journals will have to curb their proliferation while review becomes less rigorous, more fragmented and field-specific in meaning.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Base case is degraded quality plus journal consolidation rather than disruption — position for incumbent survival with worse output, not for replacement platforms taking the whole market.
insights.quote: peer review may become a less rigorous, more fragmented version of what it once was, with the practice taking on different meanings in different fields
insights.locator: With the pool of reviewers being tapped out

insights.claim: The dilution is already measurable: immunology has drifted from a standard three reviewers per manuscript toward an average closer to two, and some prominent economics journals already pay reviewers.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Two independent leading indicators — panel shrinkage and the emergence of paid review in economics — confirm the transition is underway, not hypothetical.
insights.quote: It used to be standard for three reviewers to review manuscripts, but Mack says he’s lately seen the average in immunology move closer to two.
insights.locator: There’s already evidence of these last two things happening

insights.claim: Peer review is described as too entrenched to be displaced wholesale because it underpins both career progression and public trust, yet mathematically unable to keep up if publishing continues growing at its current rate.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: An institution that cannot be replaced and cannot scale resolves through quiet quality failure — assume the reliability of published research declines rather than that the system visibly collapses.
insights.quote: So something’s going to break there at some point
insights.locator: It’s hard to envision a wholesale shift away from peer review
